I've read the call code and found what's causing each problem. Here's what's going wrong and how I'd fix it.

## 1. Answers mixing together (the main problem)

Each request runs as its own chat request at the same time as the others. That part is fine. The trouble is that **the second request also reads the whole conversation history, including your first question, which hadn't been answered yet**. So it answered both. That's why answer #2 starts with "I'm doing well, thanks!" and ends with *"I've started the fuller review… it's still processing."*

The voice model then read that out. So even after the real breakdown had arrived, it kept saying "still waiting on the fuller breakdown." When you asked "what are you waiting for?", that became a third request and re-ran the whole analysis.

**Fix:** during a call, each request answers only its own question. Questions still running elsewhere are left out of its history, or it's told plainly "these are being handled separately; don't answer or mention them." The prompt instruction is a one-line change. Leaving them out of the history is the more reliable fix. I'd do both.

## 2. Results spoken as a jumble

When results are ready, `lib/ai/voice-call-controller.ts` sends every one to the voice model at once (`flush()` empties the whole outbox). The voice model also re-labels them, which is how answer #2 got introduced as "For your first question…". It also cuts each result down to "a sentence or two", so the real analysis was mostly lost.

**Fix: one result at a time.** Send the first result, wait until Moneo has finished speaking it, then send the next. The work still runs in parallel; only the speaking waits its turn. I'd also let it read the full answer (the chat agent already keeps call answers to 1–3 spoken sentences) instead of shrinking it again.

## 3. Nested scrollbars

The captions box has its own scroll area (`max-h-56 overflow-y-auto`) inside the call page, which also scrolls. That's the double scrollbar in your screenshot. **Fix:** remove the inner scroll so there's only one, the page's, and keep it scrolled to the newest caption.

One thing to check: by "remove the scroll thing from the navigation itself", do you mean the outer page scrollbar should go too, so the orb, captions and tasks always fit on screen with no scrolling? Or just keep one scrollbar instead of two? I'd go with one scrollbar.

If that sounds right, I'll do these as three separate commits (history isolation → one-at-a-time speaking → scroll) and test against the real voice API.

input.prompt: Does GPT-Live support function tools (model writes arguments like a task description) besides client/responses delegation? Does the responses delegation target get the conversation and support custom function tools or MCP? How do multiple concurrent delegations and results (commentary/thinking append) work, and any guidance on delivering results one at a time? Quote exact event names and config fields.

result.output:
**Function tools:** Yes, under Responses delegation. You register "functions and custom tools" in `delegation.responses.tools`. The backend model produces each call, and the finished `response.output_item.done` item contains `call_id`, `name`, and `arguments`. Your application runs the function, then sends a `function_call_output` through `response.item.create` with the matching `call_id`, followed by `response.create`. The content doesn't describe the voice model itself writing task-description arguments. In client delegation, the `session.delegation.created` event carries only metadata, so your application builds the backend request.

**Context and tools for the Responses target:** It receives conversation context. The docs say "Live supplies conversation context and initiates delegated work." Custom functions and MCP are both supported. For MCP, you return approval decisions with `mcp_approval_response`, using `approval_request_id` and `approve`. Live passes your MCP `authorization` and `headers` to Responses but doesn't return them in the session configuration. Control tool use with `tool_choice` and `parallel_tool_calls`.

**Concurrent delegations and results:**
- Each delegation has its own ID from `session.delegation.created`. You can send several updates with the same client delegation ID.
- In Responses mode, the outer `delegation_id` on each `response.event` associates backend events with their delegation.
- Submit a result for every pending call before continuing. Missing results produce `tool_outputs_required` or `function_call_outputs_required`. Duplicate or mismatched results are rejected.
- You can send results before the current response completes. An accepted `response.create` waits for that completion, so don't resend it.
- A thinking or commentary append cancels all pending automatic acknowledgments in the session, including those for other delegations.
- Your application must avoid duplicate actions across overlapping delegations.

**Delivering results one at a time:**
- Send each result as soon as it is understandable on its own, as a verified chunk, using `session.commentary.append` with the same delegation ID.
- Keep each append within the 500-token limit.
- Use `session.thinking.append` for quiet progress that shouldn't be spoken.
- If your backend labels updates with a text prefix, wait for the full prefix before forwarding.
- The `session.commentary.appended` acknowledgment, matched by `client_event_id`, confirms context injection, not speech.

## Can the voice model write the prompt itself?

**Not directly.** In our current setup, when GPT-Live hands off a task, it sends only an id and no text. OpenAI's docs say the app has to work out the request from the transcript. That's why we use "whatever you said since the last hand-off", and why "can you in the meanwhile also…" got mixed up.

| Option | How it works | Good | Bad |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Smarter context for our chat agent** (recommended first) | Every request also gets the recent call transcript, marked "this is the new request; these others are already being handled". | No extra hop and no new moving parts. Our chat agent is already a strong model, so it can work out "that too" or "last month" from context. | It's still our code deciding where one request ends. |
| **B. GPT-Live's built-in hand-off to OpenAI** | GPT-Live hands off to an OpenAI model that sees the whole conversation. We give that model one function, `ask_moneo(question)`, and it writes a self-contained question that we run through `/api/chat`. | Closest to what you're asking for: a model that heard everything writes each task. | An extra model call adds about 1–2 s and some cost. There's a reported bug where this mode returns 403 for gpt-live-1. It's a bigger rewrite of the call code. |
| **C. Our own rewrite step** | A small fast model turns the transcript into a clean question before `/api/chat`. | Simple. | Extra delay, and mostly duplicates what A gets for free. |

**My recommendation:** do A now, together with speaking results one at a time and showing each full answer. Those three changes fix everything in your transcript. If requests still get split or merged wrongly after that, try B on a branch, tested against the real API first because of the 403 bug.

On delivery: each result goes out separately, with a cap of about 500 tokens per result. If two answers finish at once, the second waits until Moneo has finished speaking the first.

I looked at what OpenAI and LiveKit recommend, and at OpenAI's own demos. One point settles your question about going straight to Moneo: OpenAI's latency guidance says to **avoid extra rewrite calls**. My earlier idea (a backend model that rewrites the question, then calls `ask_moneo`, then `/api/chat`) runs two models one after the other, so I'm dropping it.

That leaves two good designs.

## Way 1: GPT-Live hands off to OpenAI, and that model *is* Moneo

GPT-Live hands each request to an OpenAI backend model (for example `gpt-6-luna` at low reasoning effort), which gets **Moneo's real tools** directly: search transactions, cash flow, make a card, and so on. When it calls a tool, the browser sends it to a small server endpoint that runs the same tool code `/api/chat` uses, and passes the result back.

**Pros**
- **Fastest path:** one model hop, and OpenAI keeps that connection warm and prepared. The backend model's answer streams straight to GPT-Live, so Moneo can start speaking sooner.
- **The model writes each task itself:** it hears the whole call, so "also check last month" and "that one" are understood, and greetings don't get sent on as tasks.
- This is the setup OpenAI suggests starting with. It's also what their chat-supervisor demo does: a voice model in front, a stronger text model with the tools behind it.

**Cons**
- **Big rewrite.** The tools are defined inside `/api/chat` today, so they'd have to move into a shared module. We'd also have to rebuild, for calls only, how answers are saved to the chat, the card rules, the "replace an earlier request" correction, and the progress labels.
- **Voice only works with OpenAI models**, and we don't control how much of the conversation the backend sees.
- **Untested risk:** the reported 403 bug with gpt-live-1 in this mode. The mode also can't be switched mid-call.

## Way 2: Keep `/api/chat` as Moneo's brain, but give it the right context

This is today's setup with three fixes:
1. **Cut requests out by timestamp.** Each hand-off comes with a timestamp, so we take the exact words the user said for that request instead of "everything since the last one". We remove the 3-second leftover-words fallback, which is what turns "hi, how are you" into a task.
2. **Send the call transcript as context**, labelled: "this is the new request; these others are already being handled; skip greetings." That lets Moneo understand "also" and "that" without answering the other questions.
3. **Speak each answer in full, one at a time, starting as it arrives.** The first sentence goes to Moneo's voice while the rest is still being written, and the next answer waits until the current one has been spoken.

**Pros**
- **Small, safe change:** one model hop, and the same agent, tools, cards, chat history and undo we already trust.
- **Any model works,** and we choose exactly what context each request sees. OpenAI says to use this mode when you need custom context selection or want to check results before they're spoken.
- It fixes every problem in your transcript directly.

**Cons**
- **Where one request ends is still our call,** and GPT-Live can still occasionally fold two requests into one hand-off.
- **First words are probably a bit slower** than Way 1, because each request starts a fresh `/api/chat` call (load history, then call the model) instead of a warm connection. Streaming the first sentence makes up some of that.

## What I'd do

**Build Way 2 now** and time how long until Moneo starts speaking. It's days less work and fixes everything you hit. In parallel, **try Way 1 on a branch** with two or three tools against the real API, to check the 403 bug and measure the speed gain. Move to Way 1 only if it's clearly faster.

On small talk: both ways handle a plain "hi" in GPT-Live itself, with no Moneo call. OpenAI's evaluation guide lists unnecessary hand-offs as a failure, and our prompt already says so. The thing actually causing it today is our leftover-words fallback, and both ways remove it.

## 1. Deciding whether something needs Moneo at all

| What the user says | Who handles it |
|---|---|
| "Hi, how are you", thanks, chit-chat | GPT-Live alone, no hand-off |
| "What are you waiting for?", "Is it done?" | GPT-Live, from the progress notes the harness quietly sends it about each running task |

The harness builds a short brief for every request:
- **This request:** the exact words, cut out by the hand-off's timestamp, minus greetings.
- **Recent call transcript:** the last few turns, so "also", "that one" and "last month" make sense.
- **Already being handled:** the other running requests, marked "don't answer or mention these". This is what fixes the mixing.
- **Already answered in this call:** short summaries, so Moneo doesn't repeat itself and can build on them.

The voice harness is built in 4 commits on `t3/voice-request-queue-and-scroll`, plus the earlier scrollbar commit. `npm test` (1145 passed), `npm run lint` and `npm run build` all pass, but **I haven't tested a live spoken call**. I can't speak into the mic from here, so the parts that depend on GPT-Live's real behaviour are only covered by unit tests with simulated events.

| Commit | What changed |
|---|---|
| `b2546ae1` | When a request runs, the other questions still running in the call are left out of its chat history. This was the cause of answer #2 re-answering #1. |
| `bc1a5c72` | Each request is now cut out by the hand-off's timestamp, and words after it go to the next request. Moneo gets a short brief with each request: recent turns, other requests still running ("don't answer these"), and what the call has already answered. It's told to skip greetings. The 3-second leftover-words fallback is gone, so "hey, how are you" never becomes a task. |
| `7e802aa7` | Results are spoken in the order they finish, one at a time. The next one waits until Moneo has finished the current one, or 20 seconds at most. "Still working on…" is checked at the moment a result goes out, so it's never out of date. |
| `9490fbcd` | GPT-Live's prompt now says to read results in full, not "a sentence or two". "What are you waiting for?", "is it done?" and "say that again" are answered from what it already has, without a new request. |
| `191bef00` | Hidden scrollbars (done earlier by the Haiku subagent). |

Three things to watch in a real call:
- **Timestamp cut:** I'm assuming the hand-off's timestamp uses the same clock as the transcript timestamps. If it doesn't, the code falls back to "everything since the last hand-off", which is how it worked before.
- **"Already spoken" check:** a result counts as spoken once Moneo has spoken at all after receiving it and then gone quiet for 0.7 seconds. A very long pause in the middle of a result could let the next one start early.
- **Requests GPT-Live merges:** with the fallback gone, if GPT-Live folds two questions into one hand-off, Moneo answers them together instead of as two tasks.

To try it, rerun your exact scenario: the September analysis, then "how much did I spend" while it's running, then "what are you waiting for".

## Why it said it couldn't confirm the loans

Moneo has no tool that reads the Wealth page. Its tools see transactions, accounts, balances, recurring payments and goals, but not assets, debts or "Lent to …" items. So it searched transactions, found payments to people, and couldn't tell whether they were loans.

**Fix:** a read-only tool that lists Wealth items (assets, debts, money lent and money borrowed) with amounts and dates. It would reuse `loadWealthItems`, the same code the Wealth page uses. Then "how much have I lent and to whom" gets the real answer: €1,250 in total, €1,000 to Bilal and €250 to Venjalin.

## Why it didn't continue after you interrupted

When you cut in, GPT-Live stopped talking, as its prompt tells it to. The part of the analysis it hadn't said yet was simply gone. Nothing in our code knows a result was cut off: once a result is handed over, we treat it as done. So after answering your loan question it had nothing left to say, and it sat waiting.

**Fix:** if you start talking while a result is being read out, the harness marks that result as cut off. Once your new question has been handed off and Moneo has gone quiet, the harness sends GPT-Live a note: "You were interrupted while giving the result for '…'; finish the part you hadn't said yet." The full result goes with the note. GPT-Live has its own transcript of what it already said, so it picks up from there instead of starting over.

The order would be: answer your interruption ("sure, checking that"), then finish the cut-off result, then say the next result when it's ready. If your interruption was "stop" or "skip that", it doesn't resume.

## How the requests and chats work

All 3 requests go into the same chat, the one the call belongs to. Each one runs on its own, at the same time as the others, and saves its own question and answer into that chat. They share the chat's history, but questions still running are left out, so answers don't get mixed together.

Each request runs separately on its own; it isn't steering. Steering would push your new message into a reply that's already being written, and here that doesn't happen:

- **Each request gets its own run:** a separate `/api/chat` call to the server, with its own model working through its own tool calls and its own entry in the request log. Three questions means three of these running side by side, and none of them waits for another.
- **What they share is only where they're saved:** the chat. Each run reads the chat's earlier messages (minus questions still running) and writes its own question and answer back into it.
